title: The mortise and tenon joint
subtitle: The standard through-joint for frames and simple furniture
excerpt: The mortise and tenon is the standard right-angle joint in British hand-tool joinery. A rectangular tongue (tenon) on one piece fits into a matching slot (mortise) in another. Once the proportions are right, it is the most reliable joint in furniture-making.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1885) vol. II, furniture joinery section; Newey and Drage, Practical Carpentry and Joinery, for the one-third rule and haunch geometry.

glossaryTerms.definition: A rectangular slot cut into a piece of timber to receive a tenon. The mortise is always cut first.
A rectangular tongue at the end of a piece of timber shaped to fit into a mortise. The tenon shoulders bear on the face of the mortise piece when the joint is assembled.
Timber dried to equilibrium moisture content for indoor use. Required for all joinery work: green timber moves as it dries and will loosen glued joints.

content.text: The
mortise
and
tenon

is the first joint to learn in hand-tool joinery. It connects a horizontal rail to a vertical post at a right angle, held by glue and the mechanical fit of the tongue in its slot. Once you can cut the proportions reliably, it makes a tight joint faster than a biscuit or domino. This instruction covers the standard through-tenon in
seasoned wood
When to use it

Any right-angle joint between two pieces of timber where strength matters: stool rails to legs, frame corners, door frames, simple tables. Not useful for thin material (under 18 mm) or for joints that need to flex after assembly.
Proportions

The one-third rule: the tenon is one-third the thickness of the rail, centred on its face. So for a 36 mm thick rail, the tenon is 12 mm thick, with 12 mm shoulders on each face. The tenon length equals the full depth of the mortise piece, for a through-tenon. The width of the tenon equals the full width of the rail minus 5 mm at each edge (the shoulders stop the joint twisting).
Cutting the mortise

Mark the mortise on the mortise piece with the marking gauge set to the tenon thickness. Mark both faces and both ends of the slot. Chop vertically into the middle of the slot with the chisel (bevel facing into the waste), working toward the ends but staying 3 mm short. Prise the waste out. Repeat from the other face, meeting in the middle. A through-mortise is cut from both faces so the fibres tear inward and the walls stay clean. Pare the walls flat with the chisel's back face against the gauge lines.
Cutting the tenon

Mark the tenon shoulders and cheeks with the marking gauge. Saw the cheeks with the tenon saw, keeping the saw on the waste side of the gauge line. Start with a few draw strokes (toward you) to establish the kerf, then saw forward at 45 degrees until the cut is established on both the face and edge, then level the saw. Saw the shoulders with the tenon saw, finishing each cut from both face and edge directions so the shoulder is square.
What a good fit looks like

The tenon should push into the mortise by hand, needing light mallet taps to close the last 5 mm. If it falls in without resistance, the cheeks need packing (a shaving of veneer glued on). If it won't enter at all, pare the cheeks in thin strokes with the chisel bevel-down, checking fit after each pass. The joint should close with the shoulders flush against the mortise face and no daylight at the joint line.
Common mistakes
Tenon too loose: the cheeks were pared past the gauge line. Pack with veneer on one or both cheeks before gluing.
Mortise walls tapered: the chisel drifted as it was driven. Pare back to the gauge lines with the chisel's back against the wall.
Shoulders not square: the tenon saw ran off-line. Mark the shoulders clearly and use a shooting board or shoulder plane to correct a small error.
Joint opens after assembly: the timber was not fully seasoned. Seasoned timber is required for all glued joinery.
